segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For you will be judged by the judgment with which you judge, and it will be measured to you by the measure with which you measure.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ and look, the beam is in your own eye?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or is there anyone among you who, when his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or when he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If you, then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in the heavens give good things to those who ask him!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So everything you want people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and spacious the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For narrow is the gate and cramped the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You will recognize them by their fruits. Do people gather grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, every good tree produces fine fruit, but the rotten tree produces bad fruit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree produce fine fruit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Every tree that does not produce fine fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So then, you will recognize them by their fruits.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of the heavens, but the one who does the will of my Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, was it not in your name that we prophesied, and in your name that we drove out demons, and in your name that we did many deeds of power?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who practice lawlessness.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a sensible man who built his house on rock.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the rain came down, and the torrents came, and the winds blew and fell upon that house, yet it did not fall, for it had been founded on rock.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on sand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the rain came down, and the torrents came, and the winds blew and battered that house, and it fell—and its fall was great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astounded at his teaching,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not like their scribes.

notes.note: The passive verbs do not name who does the judging and measuring. Most interpreters take them as a reverent way of referring to God’s judgment, a common idiom in Jewish speech of the period. They could also be read as a general observation that people are treated as they treat others.
The Greek word names a main structural timber of a building, such as a roof beam, and the word for “speck” a tiny chip of straw or wood. The contrast is a deliberately absurd exaggeration.

The phrase most naturally suggests consecrated food, such as meat from a sacrifice, which only certain people could eat. Dogs were mostly scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean animals under the Law of Moses, so both stand for those with no regard for what is sacred. Who exactly is meant is not stated and is disputed.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 21, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God’s dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. The plural is kept wherever the Greek has it.

The edition translated here reads “for” (ὅτι), parallel to verse 13. Many manuscripts and some critical editions instead read a word (τί) that makes the sentence an exclamation: “How narrow is the gate!” The sense of the saying is little affected.

The participle means “pressed in” or “squeezed”, the opposite of the “spacious” road of verse 13. The same verb is used elsewhere of people under pressure or persecution. Many translations therefore render it “hard” or “difficult”, and a hearer may have caught both senses.

The Greek is the ordinary word for “power” used of concrete acts. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the link with the word “power” stays visible.

The dismissal closely echoes the Greek version of Psalm 6:8, “Depart from me, all you who practice lawlessness.” Many older translations have “workers of iniquity” or “evildoers”. The Greek word specifically names disregard for God’s law, which sharpens the contrast with doing the Father’s will in verse 21.

Most translations have “wise”. The Greek word is not the usual term for wisdom (σοφός) but one for practical good sense and prudence, the quality of someone who thinks ahead. Standard lexica give “sensible”, “prudent” and “wise” as glosses, so the difference is one of nuance.

The word ordinarily means “rivers”. Here it refers to the sudden rush of water that fills dry streambeds in Palestine after heavy rain. Traditional versions have “floods”. “Torrents” keeps the sense of moving streams rather than standing water.

Scribes were trained experts in the Law of Moses who taught and interpreted it, typically by appeal to Scripture and received tradition. The contrast is that Jesus spoke on his own authority, as in the repeated “but I tell you” of this sermon.
